1 Introduction

B0y comparing increasingly tight human–AI coupling with canonical transitions such as chromosomes, eukaryotic cells, and multicellularity, they ask whether cooperation, division of labor, and aligned interests could eventually produce a new evolutionary individual. This is a productive question because it relocates discussion from isolated machine capability to organization across scales (
). The present article does not replace that framework or criticize it for failing to answer a different question. It offers a supplement: even if a human–AI composite acquired some properties of an evolutionary individual, what additional organization would make it a cognitive individual?
Individuality has no single accepted currency. Biological and philosophical accounts emphasize, among other things, reproduction and selection, operational closure, autonomy, informational integration, temporal persistence, and organism–environment partitioning (
;
;
;
). These criteria are relevant to human–AI composites. Yet none by itself determines whether heterogeneous information is organized into contents that can guide perception, action, inference, and evaluation across time. I therefore treat representational architecture as a domain-specific criterion of cognitive—not biological—individuality. It is privileged here because the target phenomenon is meaningful, flexible cognition: the capacity to preserve referential relations, recombine event content, compare alternatives, and revise commitments. This is a theoretical choice rather than a claim that all cognition must be explained representationally.

6 Conclusion
The MET framework identifies an important possibility: sustained human–AI cooperation may reorganize individuality at evolutionary and informational levels. A theory of cognitive individuality adds a distinct question—whether the composite maintains and revises representations as an integrated system. The proposed cross-modular criterion locates strong cognitive integration in recurrent, bidirectional, persistent, cross-domain, and corrigible interactions among generative structure, event memory, perception, affect, and social evaluation. This criterion is representational but not isolationist: representations remain embodied, environmentally scaffolded, and socially governed.
Current AI systems already exceed mere instrumentality in some settings. Memory-augmented agents, multimodal models, and stable workflows can support cognitive scaffolding, recurrent coupling, and partial informational integration. What has not been demonstrated is constitutive participation in a shared, temporally continuous, event-grounded, and normatively revisable architecture. Human–AI coevolution should therefore be understood as a graded transformation whose decisive issue is not scale alone, but the organization, control, and revision of representations across the human–machine boundary.
